title: Cost and model routing
summary: How each step picks a model and effort: task classes, starting tiers, the escalation bound, a headless spend cap and the prompt-cache lifetime.

questions.prompt: Which task classes does routing distinguish?

options.label: Explore, plan, implement, review and debug
options.tradeoff: Each class gets its own tier and effort, matching the agent roles; the most settings to reason about.

options.label: Two classes: fast and strong
options.tradeoff: Explore and implement run as fast, plan, review and debug as strong; simpler, and a group starts at its strongest member's tier.

options.label: One class per agent role
options.tradeoff: Names follow the role ids in telemetry and routing output; same tiers as the five classes, so no new saving.

questions.prompt: Which tier does each class start at?

options.label: Balanced: explore small, implement medium, plan, review and debug large
options.tradeoff: Spends on the classes where quality matters most, each at the lowest effort it allows.

options.label: Quality-first: everything but explore starts large, at higher effort
options.tradeoff: Fewer escalations and retries; the highest spend.

options.label: Cost-first: explore and implement small, the rest medium, at low effort
options.tradeoff: The lowest spend; more steps fail verification and escalate.

questions.prompt: How many times may a failed step escalate one tier before a human decides?
What is the spend cap in USD for a headless run, where the host has one?
How long is the prompt cache kept, where the host lets you set it?

options.label: One hour for the main session, five minutes for subagents
options.tradeoff: The one-hour write costs more but pays off after two reads and survives pauses; subagents are short-lived.

options.label: Five minutes everywhere
options.tradeoff: Cheaper writes; a pause of over five minutes re-reads the whole prefix at full price.

options.label: Leave the host defaults
options.tradeoff: No settings written; the cost model assumes five minutes.

decisions.title: Routing distinguishes explore, plan, implement, review and debug
decisions.body:
## Decision

Each task class is routed on its own, matching the agent roles (pack {{pack.id}}@{{pack.version}}).

## Why

Routing minimises expected total step cost among eligible models (decisions 0016, 0020, 0032); classes carry the quality bar.

decisions.title: Routing distinguishes a fast and a strong class
decisions.body:
## Decision

Explore and implement are routed as fast; plan, review and debug as strong. A group starts at the strongest tier and effort of its members (pack {{pack.id}}@{{pack.version}}).

## Why

Routing minimises expected total step cost among eligible models (decisions 0016, 0020, 0032); classes carry the quality bar.

decisions.title: Routing distinguishes one class per agent role
decisions.body:
## Decision

Each agent role is its own routing class (pack {{pack.id}}@{{pack.version}}).

## Why

Routing minimises expected total step cost among eligible models (decisions 0016, 0020, 0032); classes carry the quality bar.

decisions.title: Classes start at balanced tiers and the lowest effort they allow
decisions.body:
## Decision

Starting tiers and efforts per task class are recorded in this decision's data; verification escalates a failed step one tier up (pack {{pack.id}}@{{pack.version}}).

## Why

Routing minimises expected total step cost among eligible models (decisions 0016, 0020, 0032); classes carry the quality bar.

guardrails.title: Delegations to a role are routed by expected total step cost

frontmatter.derivation-note: Given routing picks the cheapest eligible tier by expected total step cost (0016), a delegation that bypasses the router can pick an ineligible or needlessly costly model, so the host must route it where it can.

enforcement.check: Where no hook routes the delegation, run `go-getter route --class <class> --host <host id>` and delegate with the `delegateModel` it returns
Pre-delegation hook sets the delegated model from the router, or denies when no model is eligible

guardrails.body:
## Guardrail

A delegation to a role uses the model `go-getter route` returns for its class, passed as its `delegateModel` (the value the host's delegation tool accepts): the host hook sets it where the host allows, otherwise ask the router before delegating. After the maximum number of escalations a step goes to a human.

decisions.title: A failed step escalates at most {{answer.max-escalations}} times, then a human decides
decisions.body:
## Decision

A step that fails verification moves one tier up at most {{answer.max-escalations}} times; after that it goes to a human and is never retried (pack {{pack.id}}@{{pack.version}}). The verification gate stops use the same bound.

## Why

An unbounded retry loop can burn unlimited tokens (guardrail routing-escalation-bounded).

decisions.title: Headless runs are capped at {{answer.spend-cap}} USD where the host has a cap
decisions.body:
## Decision

Headless runs pass the host's native spend-cap flag with {{answer.spend-cap}} USD; `go-getter route --headless-flags --host <id>` prints it (pack {{pack.id}}@{{pack.version}}). Hosts without a headless cap are not capped.

## Why

An unattended run has no human to notice runaway spend.

decisions.title: The prompt cache lives one hour in the main session and five minutes in subagents
decisions.body:
## Decision

Where the host has settings for it, `apply` sets the main-session prompt-cache lifetime to one hour and subagents to five minutes (pack {{pack.id}}@{{pack.version}}).

## Why

A one-hour write pays off after two reads and survives pauses (fact 0011); subagents are short-lived.

decisions.title: The prompt cache lives five minutes everywhere
decisions.body:
## Decision

Where the host has settings for it, `apply` sets every prompt-cache lifetime to five minutes (pack {{pack.id}}@{{pack.version}}).

## Why

Five-minute writes are the cheapest; a longer pause re-reads the prefix at full price.

decisions.title: The prompt-cache lifetime is left at the host defaults
decisions.body:
## Decision

`apply` writes no cache-lifetime settings; the cost model assumes five minutes (pack {{pack.id}}@{{pack.version}}).

## Why

Nothing to maintain; the host default may be shorter than a pause costs.
